results.title: Upcoming GPU Pricing Updates | DigitalOcean
highlights:
Effective August 1st, 2026, we will be updating prices on select GPUs. This change reflects strong demand for advanced GPU capacity and helps us expand reliable access to high-performance compute for customers. Even with the updated rates, DigitalOcean continues to offer some of the most competitive GPU infrastructure pricing in the market.

Below is a detailed breakdown of these upcoming changes and how they affect you.

# On-Demand GPU Price Adjustments

Effective August 1, 2026, on-demand pricing for NVIDIA and AMD GPU droplets will be updated as follows:

What this means for your bill: Any active workloads running on or after August 1, 2026 will be billed at the new rate. By continuing to access or use the services on or after August 1, 2026, you are agreeing to accept and pay the updated rates. These changes will be reflected in your total bill on September 1, 2026.

If you do not wish to continue using the service at the updated rate, you will need to take action by August 1, 2026 to destroy your GPU Droplets.

# 12-Month Reserved GPU Price Adjustments

For teams running predictable, continuous training or inference workloads, reserved plans remain the most cost-effective way to lock in lower rates. Effective August 1, 2026, we’re also adjusting our 12-month reserved pricing:

What this means for your bill: If you’re currently in a contract with us that locks in your rate, there is no change to your rate. If you choose to renew after your terms expires, your rates will be adjusted to the new 12-month reserved rate outlined above.

If you have questions about how these changes will impact your specific workloads, or if you want to explore reserving capacity, please contact our sales team—we’re here to help you find the most cost-efficient path forward.

results.title: AI Compute Demand Outpaces IREN's 480MW Build as $2.8B Contracts Close
highlights:
IREN Limited closed Monday with its order book fuller than its construction schedule can satisfy. The AI cloud provider announced $2.8 billion in new multi-year contracts with a roster of leading AI developers — and disclosed, almost as a footnote, that demand from hyperscalers, enterprises, and frontier labs now exceeds every megawatt of capacity the company has planned to build.

That demand signal matters beyond IREN's own stock price. At 480 megawatts of commissioned capacity targeted by year-end 2026 — roughly the electrical draw of 400,000 American homes — a company running out of room to sell is a concrete data point in a debate that has consumed Wall Street all year: whether the AI infrastructure buildout has overshot demand, or whether demand is still running harder than anyone can build.

...

Roughly 85% of the revised $4 billion-plus annualized run-rate revenue (ARR) target is now under contract, giving investors an unusually high degree of forward visibility for a company still in the middle of a multi-gigawatt build-out. Contracted pricing "continues to strengthen," per the press release, suggesting that available GPU capacity remains scarce relative to what potential customers want to buy.

A structural detail buried in the announcement's footnotes deserves attention from anyone evaluating IREN's capital requirements: customer prepayments covering approximately 45% of the GPU capital expenditure for those specific deployments, under contracts signed since June 1, 2026. That arrangement, if sustained, meaningfully reduces how much IREN must raise externally for each new tranche of hardware — effectively shifting a portion of the capex burden to customers who want guaranteed compute access.

...

The most consequential sentence in Monday's announcement was one of its quietest: "Demand from hyperscalers, enterprises, AI developers and frontier labs continues to exceed IREN's available and planned capacity."

For companies building frontier AI applications, securing multi-year GPU compute commitments has become a strategic necessity rather than a procurement decision. Training a large language model at the scale required to compete with the frontier requires predictable, long-horizon access to GPU clusters that cannot be bought on demand when needed — the market simply does not work that way. The hyperscale public clouds (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) offer flexibility and broad service ecosystems, but historically at prices that run 50% to 66% above what neocloud providers charge for equivalent bare-metal GPU performance. IREN's model allows customers who know their multi-year compute needs to contract for it at scale, with guaranteed capacity allocation, at rates the company says are currently moving higher rather than lower.

...

What it proves: At IREN's specific price, customer list, and contract terms, demand for contracted GPU compute capacity exceeds what IREN has planned to build through 2027. That is a real demand signal from a company with direct commercial relationships with Microsoft, NVIDIA, Perplexity, and seven other named AI developers.

What it does not prove: Whether the broader GPU rental market is supply-constrained or heading toward oversupply as hyperscalers bring their own massive internal GPU fleets online. Bloomberg reported on July 1 that Meta Platforms is developing plans to sell its surplus GPU capacity to outside customers — a move that sent neocloud stocks (including IREN, which fell roughly 6.5% that day) lower on fears of a new, debt-free competitor entering the market with hyperscale GPU inventory.

The question is structural. Meta, Microsoft, Google, and Amazon are collectively on pace to spend roughly $700 billion on AI infrastructure capital expenditures in 2026. If even a fraction of that capacity eventually becomes available to external customers, the neocloud pricing environment could shift materially. IREN's multi-year contracts, with an average term of four years, provide substantial insulation from that risk for existing contracted capacity — but approximately 15% of the $4 billion-plus ARR target remains to be contracted, and that tranche will be priced in whatever market exists when the capacity comes online.

...

Signing contracts is one deliverable. Commissioning 480 megawatts of GPU capacity by December 31, 2026 — while building toward 1.2 gigawatts in 2027 across North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific — is another category of challenge entirely. Power interconnection timelines, GPU hardware delivery schedules, and the commissioning and customer-acceptance process that must occur before revenue is recognized are all execution variables that no contract can guarantee.

results.title: The rent-side discount era is over
highlights:
On 1 July, AWS raised its GPU reservation prices for the second time this year — a Blackwell B300 reservation now runs $14.04 per GPU-hour. “Just rent it” has been this newsletter’s standing advice against a rising buy-side. That escape hatch is now closing too, and for the exact same reason.

AWS Capacity Blocks are short-term reserved ML capacity — the premium tier. Neocloud spot rates sit far below but are volatile and often sold out. The Blackwell row compares a B300 reservation to the B200 spot index (closest matched SKU). Sources: BigGo, Thunder Compute, Ornn/Silicon Data.

Here is the news, dated and specific. Effective 1 July 2026, AWS updated pricing for EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML — its short-term GPU reservation product — for the second time this year. The new US per-GPU-hour rates: $14.04 for a Blackwell B300 (P6-B300), $6.865 for an H200 (P5en), and $5.191 for an H100 (P5). AWS’s stated reason is the usual boilerplate: prices “are updated periodically based on supply and demand.”

The reason that matters is the direction. Rewind to June 2025, when AWS cut on-demand GPU instances by up to 45% — the move that anchored our rent-vs-buy break-even math and made “rent, don’t buy” the easy call. That was the tail end of a discount era. In 2026 it reversed: a January hike to Capacity Blocks, then this one. Previous-gen H100 and H200 hyperscaler rentals never got their usual post-Blackwell markdown — they stayed stubbornly flat — while Blackwell rental rates have climbed roughly 20% year-to-date. The spot market tells the same story with more drama: the Ornn B200 index whipsawed from $4.40 in January to $2.75 in February to a $6.11 intraday spike in March. Cheap, reliable GPU-hours are no longer a given.

## It’s the same shortage — one layer down

We named this disease two weeks ago. The DRAM supercycle reprices the memory in every box you might buy; the culprit is HBM, the stacked memory bolted onto every H200 and Blackwell, pulling wafer capacity away from commodity DRAM. Here is the part that closes the loop: the component actually constrained in a cloud H200 or B300 is that same HBM. HBM costs jumped ~30% in Q4 2025 alone. So the squeeze that inflates the RAM in your Strix box also inflates the lease on the datacenter card — even when the provider has silicon on the floor. Lambda, Crusoe, Nebius and FluidStack have all reported sold-out Blackwell pods for Q2 and Q3 delivery. Buy-side and rent-side are two faces of one memory bottleneck.

## Build / buy / rent

Renting still wins on cost — but by less, and watch which rate you quote. The reservation tier is where the hikes land; the neocloud spot floor (H100 ~$2.19, H200 ~$2.40) is a third of AWS’s reserved rate. If you rent, live on spot and tolerate the volatility — do not lock a long Capacity Block at $14/hr for a Blackwell you’ll use intermittently.

The real hedge is per-token API, not GPU-hours. This is the crucial split: raw GPU rental is rising, but per-token prices have not moved like the hardware — GLM-5.2 is still ~$1.40/$4.40 per Mtok. Providers who bought memory early and at scale are absorbing the squeeze inside amortized tokens. For the crown models you can’t hold locally, an API call is now a better deal than reserving the metal to run them yourself.

results.title: Why New GPU Fleets Can Go Unfunded in a Compute Shortage
highlights:
Lenders prefer contracted revenue. That is not surprising. What needs explaining is why they still rely on it when compute is expected to remain scarce. In April, SemiAnalysis argued that GPU scarcity was likely to persist and rental prices were more likely to rise than fall as token demand grew and supply tightened. Even if that forecast is right, a shortage across the market does not guarantee that one fleet securing a loan will stay rented.

USD.AI’s pipeline makes the problem visible. In June, its team told me customers were waiting for GPUs or paying premiums to skip the line. Yet eight of its nine upcoming loans, representing 98 percent of the money, were backed by signed customer contracts. The only exception involved GPUs already earning rental revenue. This snapshot cannot show rejected applications or prove that USD.AI requires contracts, but it shows the gap between market demand and revenue a lender can count on from one fleet.

The lender must predict both the price each GPU-hour will earn and the number of hours the fleet will sell before the operator has rental history. Lenders handle that uncertainty with long customer contracts, an established company’s financial history, or another company’s promise to pay.

...

The loan may begin before the GPUs are installed and remain outstanding for three years or longer. Even if the broader shortage persists, demand for this fleet can weaken during the loan.

Demand may also be for a different fleet. Customers care about the chip, cluster size, networking, location, and whether the operator can keep it running. Even a customer that chooses the fleet may not commit for as long as the lender needs. SemiAnalysis reports that companies renting GPUs to run AI products often want capacity for one year or less because they cannot predict demand for their own products.

...

Its lending policy lists annual interest rates of 7 to 9 percent when a highly rated customer has signed a long contract. A long contract with a less creditworthy customer costs 10 to 12 percent. A loan supported by short-term rentals costs 12 to 15 percent.

Under USD.AI’s published policy, borrowers relying on short-term rentals must show documented history of on-demand revenue. Projected rentals alone are not enough. USD.AI also lends no more than 80 percent of the hardware cost, requires cash for three months of loan payments, and expects repayment over three years.

...

One unknown is the price those future rentals will earn. Can a market price make these loans easier?

A forward price solves one variable

The compute market is beginning to publish prices for future GPU rentals. Silicon Data launched a forward curve in April 2026 using observed agreements lasting up to three years. CME and ICE have announced financial contracts tied to rental-price indexes. If those contracts attract enough trading, an operator could protect itself against a broad fall in prices.

The same fleet can earn less because hourly prices fall or because fewer hours are rented.

A price-index futures contract protects against a broad decline in rental prices. It does not guarantee how many hours this fleet rents.

Suppose the market rental price stays at $3 per hour, but a young operator loses its main customer and half its GPUs sit idle. The price index has not fallen, so the futures contract does not pay. The operator’s revenue still drops by half.

A contract for a fixed number of GPU-hours could cover the missing variable. If a buyer or financial firm promised to pay for those hours over several years, the lender would still receive payments when ordinary renters did not show up. The risk would move to whoever made the promise. In practice, this would resemble standardized offtake.

...

In every example, the lender relies on more than the general compute shortage: past rental revenue, an established company’s financial history, or an outside promise of revenue. The unresolved case is a young operator with none of the three.

...

A capable operator serving them may face real demand without having years of payments locked in before the fleet is built.

Forward prices estimate what each rented hour may earn, not how many hours the operator will sell. Because the operator is new, there is no past rental performance to examine. A specialist lender may still investigate the operator and require more cash, but the public record does not reveal a method another lender could apply to the next one.

...

If the demand described at the start persists and existing fleets remain full, the market will need more capacity. But some fleets may go unbuilt even if they could have served real demand, because customer commitments are shorter than the loans. The evidence here shows that mismatch, not how much capacity it prevents.

results.title: 一天吃透一个行业342：算力租赁，附相关股票名单_新浪财经_新浪网
highlights:
一、 行业核心变化：从"卖硬件"到"卖服务"，算力租赁进入放量兑现期

算力租赁的本质是AI时代的"算力电厂"——中游服务商采购GPU服务器，以按需付费、弹性租用的模式向下游AI企业提供算力资源，是连接上游硬件与下游应用的核心桥梁。

当前行业正经历三重共振，从概念炒作进入业绩兑现阶段：

- 供需缺口持续扩大：据中国信通院数据，2026年一季度国内算力租赁市场规模达 680亿元，同比增长62%，预计全年突破 2600亿元。更关键的数据是，国内AI算力需求同比大增 417%，而供给增速仅 128%，供不应求格局明确。
- 租赁价格持续上涨：英伟达Blackwell系列芯片单小时租金已涨至 4.08美元，较2月上涨48%。H100一年期合约租金从2025年末约1.7美元/GPU·小时的低位持续修复至约2.4美元，涨幅达35.6%。
- 百亿级大单密集落地：东阳光年内已斩获三笔百亿级算力订单，合计金额达 390-460亿元。行云科技获客户追加租金 28.79亿元，较原金额上调79%。这些长单验证了下游客户"提前锁定优质算力资源"的迫切需求。
- 标志性事件佐证算力紧张：7月19日，Kimi因算力紧缺宣布暂停C端新用户订阅，将全部算力投入已有用户服务。这直观反映了当前高端算力供不应求的紧张局面。

...

三、 风险提示：行业同样面临不确定性

在关注行业高景气的同时，也需留意潜在风险：

1. 芯片供应政策扰动：美国对华科技封锁加码，芯片进口政策变化可能影响算力租赁企业的"卡源"稳定性。
2. 老款芯片清库存冲击：随着英伟达Rubin、Blackwell等新品量产，老款GPU可能降价清库存，冲击现有租赁价格体系。
3. 行业同质化竞争：当前算力租赁企业数量快速增长，市场对订单的可持续性和不同企业的竞争力仍存在难以区分的问题。

results.title: GPU Clouds Become a Hyperscaler Utility · Slicast
highlights:
# GPU Clouds Become a Hyperscaler Utility

Vertical integration and inter-hyperscaler leasing are pricing third-party GPU vendors out of strategic importance.

Hyperscalers have stopped competing for GPU capacity and started building it. Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google announced $50+ billion in owned infrastructure this month alone: Meta's Louisiana megafacility, OpenAI's $20–30 billion Georgia campus, Anthropic's $19 billion TeraWulf contract, and a $10 billion inter-hyperscaler lease between Meta and Anthropic. Simultaneously, $40 billion in institutional capital (MGX, AIP, BlackRock) closed the Aligned Data Centers acquisition, while Japan announced its sovereign AI infrastructure consortium with NVIDIA. The pattern is unmistakable: hyperscalers and governments are consolidating control of AI infrastructure. Third-party GPU vendors are no longer platforms—they're becoming utilities.

The neocloud market is pricing this correctly. CoreWeave, Nebius, and IREN have lost 30–61% market cap this month as investors recognize the structural problem: when hyperscalers control their own supply, third-party vendors lose leverage. NVIDIA's 9.3% stake in Nebius (shares up 19%) reads as triage, not confidence—the chip giant is placing a bet that at least one independent distributor survives. Hut 8 and TeraWulf have adapted by locking into long-term fixed contracts with hyperscalers, not competing as generalist cloud providers. CoreWeave's $249 billion debt burden is now under systemic scrutiny. GPU supply pluralism (AMD's $5 billion Anthropic partnership, NVIDIA's Vera production) validates chip alternatives, but pluralism only matters if third-party vendors can still compete.

...

If software efficiency, lean teams, and open-weight models close performance gaps faster than hyperscalers can deploy $20–30 billion megafacilities, the race is no longer ... It's about intelligence-per-GPU and control of the distribution layer.

results.title: DigitalOcean (NYSE: DOCN) Raises On-Demand GPU Prices by Roughly 30% Starting August 1
highlights:
Key Highlights

- DigitalOcean is raising on-demand prices for select Nvidia and AMD GPUs by roughly 30%, effective August 1.
- H100 pricing will increase from $3.39 to $4.41 per hour.
- H200 pricing will rise from $3.44 to $4.47 per hour, and AMD's MI300X from $1.99 to $2.59.
- Existing reserved contracts keep current rates until renewal; new and renewed 12-month plans move to the higher pricing.

DigitalOcean ($DOCN) is raising on-demand prices for select Nvidia and AMD graphics processing units by roughly 30%, starting August 1, citing strong demand for advanced AI compute.

## What Happened

Under the new pricing, on-demand access to Nvidia's H100 chip will increase from $3.39 to $4.41 per hour. The H200, Nvidia's more advanced successor chip, will rise from $3.44 to $4.47 per hour.

AMD's MI300X accelerator will see its on-demand rate increase from $1.99 to $2.59 per hour, a comparable percentage increase to the two Nvidia chips.

The company said the price increases are being driven by strong demand for advanced AI compute capacity.

## Market Reaction

Existing reserved contracts will keep their current rates until renewal, meaning customers already locked into reserved pricing agreements will not see an immediate cost increase.

New and renewed 12-month plans, however, will move to the higher pricing, extending the roughly 30% increase beyond on-demand usage to longer-term commitments signed or renewed after the change takes effect.

...

The August 1 effective date gives existing on-demand customers a defined window before the new rates take hold, while the shift for new and renewed 12-month plans suggests the higher pricing is intended to apply broadly across DigitalOcean's GPU compute offerings going forward.

results.title: 【SMM算力日报】乌兰察布96台H20入市月租3.7万__上海有色网
highlights:
### 乌兰察布96台H20 96G八卡入市，月租3.7-3.8万，居间层级混杂需甄别一手货源；WAIC期间某厂商透露获英伟达4060/4090/5090供应，华为生态未对其开放；另一国产GPU厂商称英伟达转国产适配周期难确定；服务器内存经销商批量出货覆盖三星/SK/长鑫多品牌。

SMM 7月21日讯：

乌兰察布96台H20入市 月租3.7-3.8万元

SMM获悉，乌兰察布地区近日投放96台H20 96G八卡服务器，一年起租，月租报价3.7至3.8万元。市场人士反映，该批资源出现多方同时推广现象，居间层级混杂，租赁方需注意甄别一手货源。H20虽在浮点计算性能与互联带宽上有所削减，但中国大陆合规供应与CUDA生态兼容仍为其核心竞争优势。

WAIC现场：英伟达消费级GPU供应通道仍存 国产生态门槛高

WAIC大会期间，某厂商透露其目前与英伟达保持合作关系，能够获得4060、4090、5090等消费级GPU芯片供应。当被问及是否与国产厂商有合作时，该厂商明确表示国产生态开放有门槛。另一国产GPU厂商则指出，当前企业从英伟达转向国产GPU需综合考量需求体量和迁移时间窗口，由于不同场景下的适配工作量差异较大，难以给出统一的适配完成时间。

...

某服务器配件经销商近日连续出货服务器内存条，覆盖三星、SK海力士、镁光、长鑫等品牌，规格涵盖32G至128G DDR4/DDR5多频段。其中三星64G 6400MHz含税报价15700元打包260根，三星96G 6400MHz含税26700元，国产长鑫64G 5600MHz全新条报价14600元（50根）。该经销商同时透露可供应显卡及CPU等配件。

SMM分析： H20作为英伟达对华合规供应主力型号，乌兰察布96台批量入市将缓解国内合规算力供给压力，但多方居间推广折射出渠道层级过深的问题。WAIC期间两条信息共同指向一个现实：英伟达消费级GPU供应通道仍在运转，而国产替代在生态适配和合作伙伴准入两个维度均存在障碍，短期内难以形成规模化替代效应。

results.title: 「日本のAI、意外な実需が製造業」GMOインターネット 武田氏｜BUSINESS NETWORK
highlights:
2024年11月に開始した「GMO GPUクラウド」は2025年夏から引き合いが急激に増え、9月に単月黒字に転換しました。現在はリソースの空きがほとんどない状況で、市場全体でGPUが不足しています。

顧客層については、当初はLLMの開発・学習用途を想定していました。ところが実際には、日本のLLM開発スケールは世界と比べて小さく、大量に使い続けるお客様はそれほど多くなかったというのが正直なところです。

意外な形で存在感を示したのが製造業です。もともとHPCを使っていた研究開発部門が、GPUクラウドへの移行に関心を示しています。もう1つ、大きな発見だったのが自動運転分野です。映像データの大量収集・分析には、膨大なGPUリソースが必要になります。自動運転システムを開発するスタートアップ、チューリングと4年間の長期契約を締結したほか、別の自動運転開発会社からも打診をいただいています。

次に、マネージドサービスでの提供です。一般的なGPUクラウドはベアメタルのサーバーをそのまま貸し出すだけで、設定や運用はユーザー任せが多いのですが、それだとAIエンジニアがインフラ管理にも時間を取られてしまいます。我々は当初からマネージドサービスとして展開しており、「使い勝手がいいから選んだ」という言葉を最も多くいただいています。

今後の市場展望ですが、GPU不足はしばらく続くと見ています。OpenAIをはじめとした大手がケタ違いの規模で調達を進めていて、ハイパースケーラーでさえ日本向けのリソースをOpenAIに回すように指示されているという話も耳にします。

現在のGPUクラウドは福岡のデータセンターに置いています。九州電力の電気料金の安さと、当社のエンジニアが北九州に集積していることが理由です。今後、別のエリアに展開するにあたっても、電力コストとエンジニアを配置できるかどうかが判断の軸になります。ネットワーク遅延の課題が技術的に解消されていくなら、データセンター分散化の観点からも地方展開に積極的に取り組んでいきたいです。
